subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 16! In this unit you will discover the hidden rules that keep all of mathematics fair, consistent and reliable. These rules are called the laws of arithmetic, and they decide the order in which we carry out calculations and how we are allowed to rearrange numbers to make our work easier. Just as the traffic in Mogadishu only flows safely when every driver follows the same rules of the road, a calculation only gives one trustworthy answer when everyone follows the same rules of arithmetic.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 6 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Apply the order of operations (BODMAS / BIDMAS) to evaluate expressions with several operations.
Use brackets, including nested brackets, to control the order of a calculation.
Apply the commutative law for addition and multiplication, and explain why subtraction and division are not commutative.
Apply the associative law for addition and multiplication to group numbers efficiently.
Apply the distributive law, a × (b + c) = (a × b) + (a × c), and use it in reverse to factor out a common number.
Choose the smartest law to simplify a calculation and do more of it in your head.
Translate word problems into expressions and check answers using a second method and estimation.

concepts.title: The Order of Operations (BODMAS)
concepts.explanation:
BODMAS is the agreed order for a calculation with several operations:

B – Brackets (also called parentheses) are always done first.

O – Orders (powers and roots, also called indices) come next.

DM – Division and Multiplication, worked from left to right.

AS – Addition and Subtraction, worked from left to right.

You may also meet BIDMAS (Brackets, Indices, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction) or the American PEMDAS. Do not let the different names confuse you – they all describe exactly the same order. The one point learners forget most often is that division and multiplication sit at the same level, so you simply take them as they come from left to right; the same is true for addition and subtraction.

Why this particular order? It is not a random choice made to trick students. Multiplication and division are really repeated addition and repeated sharing, so mathematicians treat them as ‘stronger’ operations that bind more tightly to the numbers around them. Doing them before addition and subtraction keeps expressions unambiguous. Consider 2 + 3 × 4. Following BODMAS we multiply first: 2 + (3 × 4) = 2 + 12 = 14. If instead we wrongly worked left to right we would get (2 + 3) × 4 = 5 × 4 = 20. Only 14 is correct, because only 14 follows the agreed rule that everyone in the world shares.

Let us walk through three examples carefully, showing every step just as you should on paper.

Example A: 15 − 3 × 2 + 8. There is a subtraction, a multiplication and an addition. Multiplication first: 3 × 2 = 6, giving 15 − 6 + 8. Now work the addition and subtraction left to right: 15 − 6 = 9, then 9 + 8 = 17.

Example B: 24 ÷ 6 + 2 × 3. Division and multiplication are at the same level, so do them left to right before the addition. 24 ÷ 6 = 4 and 2 × 3 = 6, giving 4 + 6 = 10.

Example C: 5 + 2 × 3 − 4 ÷ 2. Deal with the multiplication and division first: 2 × 3 = 6 and 4 ÷ 2 = 2, giving 5 + 6 − 2. Then left to right: 5 + 6 = 11, then 11 − 2 = 9.
concepts.example: The order of operations appears everywhere in real life: working out a shopping bill after a discount and tax, calculating how many bricks Hassan needs for a wall, scaling up a bariis recipe for a large iftar gathering, or working out the profit on a market stall. Whenever more than one operation meets in a single sum, BODMAS keeps you safe.

concepts.title: The Power of Brackets
concepts.explanation:
Brackets are the most powerful symbols in an expression because they let us override the standard order of operations. Whatever sits inside a pair of brackets must be worked out first, no matter what operations surround it. In this way brackets act like a traffic officer at a busy Nairobi junction, waving one calculation through ahead of all the others.

Look at how brackets can completely change a result. Without brackets, 3 + 4 × 2 follows BODMAS: the multiplication first, 3 + 8 = 11. But with brackets, (3 + 4) × 2 forces the addition first: 7 × 2 = 14. The very same numbers and operations give two different answers, and the brackets alone decide which one we mean.

Brackets are not only about changing the order – they can also make a calculation easier even when they do not change the answer. Suppose Farah must work out 25 × 4 + 25 × 6. She could plod through it as 100 + 150 = 250. Or she could notice the shared 25 and rewrite it as 25 × (4 + 6) = 25 × 10 = 250. The second route is far kinder to do in your head. You will meet this idea again as the distributive law in Concept 5.

Sometimes we need brackets inside brackets, called nested brackets. The rule is simple: always start with the innermost brackets and work outwards. Take 3 × (2 + (5 − 1)). First the innermost bracket: 5 − 1 = 4, giving 3 × (2 + 4). Next the remaining bracket: 2 + 4 = 6, giving 3 × 6. Finally: 3 × 6 = 18. Peeling brackets from the inside out is like unwrapping the smallest parcel hidden inside a larger one.
concepts.example: Brackets are also essential when we turn words into mathematics. ‘Add 5 to a number, then multiply the result by 3’ becomes (n + 5) × 3, because the whole sum n + 5 must be multiplied. But ‘multiply a number by 3, then add 5’ becomes 3n + 5, a completely different calculation. Getting the brackets right is how we say precisely what we mean, so that nobody misreads the instruction.

concepts.title: The Commutative Law
concepts.explanation:
The commutative law is the most intuitive of the three great laws. It says that for addition and multiplication, the order of the numbers does not change the answer. In symbols, for any two numbers a and b:

Addition: a + b = b + a, for example 7 + 3 = 3 + 7 = 10.

Multiplication: a × b = b × a, for example 6 × 4 = 4 × 6 = 24.

Why does this help? Because it gives you the freedom to rearrange numbers into an order that is easier to work with. If Omar has to calculate 3 × 47, he may find 47 × 3 quicker to picture. If Zahra faces 8 + 97, she can flip it to 97 + 8 and simply count on eight to reach 105. The answer is guaranteed to be the same, so you are always allowed to choose the friendlier order.

It is just as important to know where the commutative law does not apply. Subtraction and division are not commutative. Order matters completely for them: 10 − 3 = 7 but 3 − 10 = −7, and 12 ÷ 3 = 4 but 3 ÷ 12 = 0.25. This is why you must always keep subtraction and division in the order the problem gives you. Think of it like putting on socks and shoes: socks then shoes is fine, but shoes then socks is a very different result.
concepts.example: You can see commutativity all around you. Whether Maryam buys 3 bags of dates at 5 shillings each or 5 bags at 3 shillings each, if the totals match the commutative law is at work. Whether a cook adds two cups of flour then one cup of sugar, or one cup of sugar then two cups of flour, the mixture ends up the same. Whether Ibrahim walks 30 km north then 20 km east, or 20 km east then 30 km north, he still arrives at the same corner of the map.

concepts.title: The Associative Law
concepts.explanation:
The associative law is about grouping. It says that when three or more numbers are all added, or all multiplied, the way we group them with brackets does not change the answer. In symbols, for any three numbers a, b and c:

Addition: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c). For example (2 + 3) + 4 = 5 + 4 = 9 and 2 + (3 + 4) = 2 + 7 = 9.

Multiplication: (a × b) × c = a × (b × c). For example (2 × 3) × 4 = 6 × 4 = 24 and 2 × (3 × 4) = 2 × 12 = 24.

Be careful not to mix this up with the commutative law. Commutative is about order (which number comes first); associative is about grouping (which pair you combine first). They are close cousins but they are not the same idea.

The associative law is a gift for mental maths, because it lets you group the easy pair first. Take 25 × 7 × 4. Working left to right you would face 175 × 4 = 700, which is awkward. But by grouping cleverly, (25 × 4) × 7 = 100 × 7 = 700 – far easier, because 25 × 4 = 100 is a friendly number. In the same way, 8 + 47 + 2 becomes (8 + 2) + 47 = 10 + 47 = 57, and 5 × 23 × 2 becomes (5 × 2) × 23 = 10 × 23 = 230.
concepts.example: As with commutativity, the associative law applies only to addition and multiplication. Subtraction and division are not associative: (10 − 3) − 2 = 5 but 10 − (3 − 2) = 9, and (12 ÷ 3) ÷ 2 = 2 but 12 ÷ (3 ÷ 2) = 8. So you may only regroup freely when every operation between the numbers is an addition, or every one is a multiplication.

concepts.title: The Distributive Law
concepts.explanation: The distributive law is the most powerful law of all, because it links multiplication with addition and subtraction. It tells us that multiplying a number by a sum is the same as multiplying by each part and then adding. In symbols, for any three numbers a, b and c: a × (b + c) = (a × b) + (a × c), and a × (b − c) = (a × b) − (a × c). Let us check that it really works. 5 × (10 + 3): the direct route is 5 × 13 = 65; the distributive route is 5 × 10 + 5 × 3 = 50 + 15 = 65. They match. 7 × (20 − 2): direct route 7 × 18 = 126; distributive route 7 × 20 − 7 × 2 = 140 − 14 = 126. They match, confirming the law works for subtraction too.
concepts.example: Why does it work? Picture a rectangle, the way land is measured for a farm outside Garissa. Suppose it is 5 metres wide and (10 + 3) metres long. You can find the area in one piece as 5 × 13 = 65 square metres, or you can split it into two rectangles – one 5 × 10 and one 5 × 3 – giving 50 + 15 = 65 square metres. Both describe the very same field, so both give the same area. That picture is the heart of the distributive law.

concepts.title: Using the Laws Together to Simplify
concepts.explanation:
The real power comes when you combine the order of operations with all three laws to make a hard calculation simple. A good mathematician looks at an expression before diving in and asks, ‘Is there a smarter path?’ Very often there is.

When you meet a complex expression, follow this systematic plan: first identify all the brackets and operations; then apply BODMAS carefully; then look for chances to use the commutative, associative or distributive laws to simplify; work step by step, writing each stage clearly; and finally check your answer with a different method if you can.

Example: 3 × (4 + 2) − 5 × (7 − 3). Brackets first: 3 × 6 − 5 × 4. Multiplication next: 18 − 20. Subtraction last: 18 − 20 = −2. Notice the answer is a negative number, which is perfectly allowed.

Example: 2 × (3 + 4 × 5) − 6. Inside the bracket we must still obey BODMAS, so the multiplication comes before the addition: 4 × 5 = 20, giving 3 + 20 = 23 inside the bracket. Now 2 × 23 − 6 = 46 − 6 = 40.

Example: 7 × 15 + 7 × 5. Rather than doing two multiplications, factor out the 7: 7 × (15 + 5) = 7 × 20 = 140. Example: 25 × 8 × 4. Rearrange with the commutative and associative laws to make a round number: 25 × 4 × 8 = 100 × 8 = 800. Each of these shows how a clever choice of law replaces heavy arithmetic with something you can do in seconds.

Here is one more beautiful example of strategic grouping. To add 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 + 13 + 15, do not crawl from left to right. Pair the numbers from the outside in: (1 + 15) + (3 + 13) + (5 + 11) + (7 + 9) = 16 + 16 + 16 + 16 = 64. The commutative and associative laws make this rearrangement legal, and it turns a long sum into a single easy multiplication, 4 × 16.

You have now met the full toolkit: the order of operations (BODMAS), the power of brackets, and the commutative, associative and distributive laws. These ideas are not separate islands – they work as a team. BODMAS keeps every calculation unambiguous. Brackets let you take control of the order when you need to. The commutative and associative laws let you rearrange and regroup numbers into friendlier shapes. The distributive law lets you break a hard multiplication apart, or pull a shared number out of a sum.
concepts.example: The habit to build is this: pause before you calculate, and look for the smartest route. When Aisha needs 25 × 8 × 4, she does not reach for a long algorithm – she rearranges to 100 × 8. When Yusuf must find 6 × 47, he splits it into 6 × 40 + 6 × 7. When Khadija checks a bill, she uses BODMAS to keep the discount and tax in the right order. Each time you choose a law wisely, your number sense grows stronger, and the algebra waiting in Stage 7 will feel like a familiar friend rather than a stranger. Now let us practise together with fully worked examples.

methods.title: How to evaluate an expression
steps: Do everything inside brackets first (innermost first if nested).
Work out any orders (powers and roots).
Do division and multiplication, left to right.
Do addition and subtraction, left to right.
Check your answer with a second method if you can.

methods.title: How to use the distributive law for mental maths
steps: Split the awkward number into an easy sum or difference, such as 47 = 40 + 7 or 99 = 100 − 1.
Multiply the outside number by each part.
Add or subtract the two results.

methods.title: How to factor out a common number
methods.example: Factor out the common number in 6 × 9 + 6 × 4.
steps: Look for the same number multiplying two or more terms.
Write that number outside a bracket.
Put the remaining parts inside the bracket, then simplify.

methods.title: Using the commutative and associative laws
steps: Rearrange the order (commutative) and regroup (associative) to make a round number: 2 × 5 × 39 = (2 × 5) × 39 = 10 × 39 = 390.
Multiplying by 10 is far easier than multiplying by 39 directly.
Check by multiplying the original three numbers in their original order — you should get the same answer, 390.

methods.title: Distributive law for mental maths
methods.example: Work out 8 × 34 without a written algorithm.
steps: Split 34 into 30 + 4 and distribute: 8 × 34 = 8 × 30 + 8 × 4 = 240 + 32 = 272.
Multiply each part separately before adding the two results together.
Check by multiplying 8 × 34 directly (or on paper) to confirm you also get 272.

methods.title: Factoring out a common number
steps: Every term shares the factor 15, so pull it out: 15 × (7 + 3 + 10) = 15 × 20 = 300.
Factoring turns three multiplications into one.
Check by multiplying the bracket back out: 15 × 7 + 15 × 3 + 15 × 10 should still total 300.

workedExamples.title: A three-operation BODMAS sum
workedExamples.solution: The multiplication is the strongest operation here, so do it first: 4 × 3 = 12, giving 20 − 12 + 7. Now work the addition and subtraction left to right: 20 − 12 = 8, then 8 + 7 = 15.

workedExamples.title: Division and multiplication together
workedExamples.solution: Division and multiplication sit at the same level, so complete both before adding. 36 ÷ 9 = 4 and 5 × 2 = 10, giving 4 + 10 = 14.

workedExamples.title: Nested brackets
workedExamples.solution: Start with the innermost bracket: 2 + 3 = 5, giving 4 × (10 − 5). Next the remaining bracket: 10 − 5 = 5, giving 4 × 5. Finally 4 × 5 = 20.

workedExamples.title: Using the commutative and associative laws
workedExamples.solution: Rearrange the order (commutative) and regroup (associative) to make a round number: 2 × 5 × 39 = (2 × 5) × 39 = 10 × 39 = 390. Multiplying by 10 is far easier than multiplying by 39 directly.

workedExamples.title: Factoring out a common number
workedExamples.solution: Every term shares the factor 15, so pull it out: 15 × (7 + 3 + 10) = 15 × 20 = 300. Factoring turns three multiplications into one.

workedExamples.title: A mixed expression with brackets
workedExamples.solution: Brackets first: 5 × 8 − 3 × 4. Multiplication next: 40 − 12. Subtraction last: 40 − 12 = 28.

workedExamples.title: Translating words with brackets
workedExamples.prompt: Halima thinks of a number, adds 6, then multiplies the result by 4. Write this as an expression and work it out if her number is 7.
workedExamples.solution: ‘Adds 6, then multiplies the result by 4’ means the whole sum must be multiplied, so we need brackets: (n + 6) × 4. With n = 7 this is (7 + 6) × 4 = 13 × 4 = 52. Without the brackets, 7 + 6 × 4 would wrongly give 31, a different answer entirely.

workedExamples.title: Use the distributive law to work out in your head
workedExamples.prompt: Use the distributive law to work out in your head: a) 6 × 23 b) 8 × 45 c) 9 × 99.

workedExamples.title: Factor out the common number
workedExamples.prompt: Factor out the common number: a) 4 × 13 + 4 × 7 b) 9 × 6 + 9 × 4.

workedExamples.title: Working through nested brackets
workedExamples.solution: Start with the innermost bracket: 4 + 2 = 6, giving 3 × (12 − 6). Next the remaining bracket: 12 − 6 = 6, giving 3 × 6. Finally 3 × 6 = 18.

workedExamples.title: Place one pair of brackets in 12 − 4 × 2 so that the…
workedExamples.prompt: Place one pair of brackets in 12 − 4 × 2 so that the answer becomes 16.
workedExamples.solution: Placing brackets around the first two numbers gives (12 − 4) × 2 = 8 × 2 = 16, which matches the target answer.

activities.title: The BODMAS Card Challenge
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and small cards or scraps of paper.
steps: Write the numbers 1 to 9 on separate cards, and write the four operation signs +, −, ×, ÷ and a pair of brackets on other cards.
Deal yourself three number cards and two operation cards, then build an expression.
Solve it carefully using BODMAS, writing each step.
Now add a pair of brackets somewhere and see how the answer changes. Can you make the answer as large as possible? As small as possible?
This game trains you to see how the order of operations and brackets shape every result.

activities.title: The Rectangle Area Investigation (Distributive Law)
activities.materials: squared paper (or draw your own grid), a pencil and a ruler.
steps: Draw a rectangle 6 squares tall and 13 squares wide. Count or calculate its area: 6 × 13.
Now draw a line to split the width 13 into 10 + 3, making two smaller rectangles.
Find the area of each smaller rectangle: 6 × 10 and 6 × 3.
Add the two areas and check they match your first answer. You have just proved 6 × 13 = 6 × 10 + 6 × 3!
Try it again with a different rectangle, such as 8 × 12 split into 8 × 10 + 8 × 2.

activities.title: Mental Maths Speed Game
activities.materials: a family member or friend, and a timer or clock.
steps: One player calls out a multiplication like 6 × 48 or 7 × 99.
The other player must solve it out loud using the distributive law (for example, 6 × 48 = 6 × 50 − 6 × 2).
Score a point for each correct answer solved this way within ten seconds.
Swap roles after five turns. The player with more points wins the round.
This game shows how the laws of arithmetic turn hard sums into quick mental ones.

activities.title: Grouping with Market Stones (Associative Law)
activities.materials: a big handful of stones, beans or bottle caps to act as ‘shillings’.
steps: Set out three piles, for example 25, 17 and 75 stones.
Add them by grouping the two that make a round number first: (25 + 75) + 17.
Now add them in a different grouping, such as 25 + (17 + 75), and check you get the same total.
Talk about why the grouping did not change the answer – this is the associative law of addition.

activities.title: Bracket Detective (Family Puzzle)
activities.materials: paper and pencil for each player.
steps: Write an expression with no brackets, such as 2 + 3 × 4 − 1.
Challenge your family to place one pair of brackets to reach a target answer you choose (for example, make it equal 19).
Everyone shows their bracket placement and checks it with BODMAS.
Take turns being the puzzle-setter. The more surprising the target, the better!

activities.title: The Laws Poster Investigation
activities.materials: a large sheet of paper and coloured pens.
steps: Divide your poster into four boxes: Order of Operations, Commutative Law, Associative Law, Distributive Law.
In each box, write the rule in your own words and draw a clear example.
Add one real-life picture for each law, such as a rectangle field for the distributive law.
Show your poster to your teacher, a family member, or your AI tutor, and explain each law aloud. Teaching it proves you truly understand it.

After your activities, talk or write about these questions: Which law was the most surprising to discover? Which activity made the distributive law clearest for you? Where in everyday life did you notice one of these laws at work? What would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher or your AI tutor at your next session.

rules.title: The Order of Operations (BODMAS)
rules.text: B – Brackets first. O – Orders (powers and roots) next. DM – Division and Multiplication, left to right. AS – Addition and Subtraction, left to right.

rules.title: Commutative Law
rules.text: Addition: a + b = b + a, for example 7 + 3 = 3 + 7. Multiplication: a × b = b × a, for example 6 × 4 = 4 × 6. It does NOT work for subtraction or division.

rules.title: Associative Law
rules.text: Addition: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c). Multiplication: (a × b) × c = a × (b × c). It is about grouping, and only works for addition or multiplication.

rules.title: Distributive Law
rules.text: a × (b + c) = (a × b) + (a × c). a × (b − c) = (a × b) − (a × c). In reverse it lets you factor out a shared number.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Place one pair of brackets in 12 − 4 × 2 so that the answer becomes 16.

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The innermost bracket is 8 − 3 = 5, giving 4 × (5 + 5) − 6 = 4 × 10 − 6. Then 4 × 10 = 40, so 40 − 6 = 34.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Zahra says 3 × (4 + 5) is the same as 3 × 4 + 5. Is she right? Explain her mistake and give the correct answer.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: No, she is not right. The brackets mean the 3 must multiply the whole sum: 3 × (4 + 5) = 3 × 9 = 27. Her version, 3 × 4 + 5 = 12 + 5 = 17, only multiplies the 4 and forgets to multiply the 5, so it gives a different, incorrect answer. The correct answer is 27.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Add 5 + 10 + 15 + 20 + 25 + 30 by pairing cleverly. Show your pairs and the total.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Pair the numbers to make equal sums: (5 + 30) + (10 + 25) + (15 + 20) = 35 + 35 + 35 = 3 × 35 = 105.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Use the distributive law to calculate 15 × 21 by splitting 21 into 20 + 1.
Explain the key idea in Using the Laws Together to Simplify.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The real power comes when you combine the order of operations with all three laws to make a hard calculation simple. A good mathematician looks at an expression before diving in and asks, 'Is there a smarter path?' Very often there is. When you meet a complex expression, follow this systematic plan: first identify all the brackets and operations; then apply BODMAS carefully; then look for chances to use the commutative, associative or distributive laws to simplify; work step by step, writing each stage clearly; and finally check your answer using a second method or an estimate.

questions.question: Calculate 2 × 39 × 5 the smart way.
questions.hint: Work it out step by step, using the Unit 16 methods.
questions.explanation: Rearrange the order (commutative) and regroup (associative) to make a round number: 2 × 5 × 39 = (2 × 5) × 39 = 10 × 39 = 390. Multiplying by 10 is far easier than multiplying by 39 directly.

questions.question: Work out 8 × 34 without a written algorithm.

questions.question: Which statement is a correct example of the commutative law?
questions.hint: Check whether swapping the order still gives the same answer.
questions.explanation: The commutative law says order does not matter for addition and multiplication. 8 + 5 = 13 and 5 + 8 = 13, so this is correct. Subtraction and division are not commutative, so the other options are false.

questions.question: Which statement correctly shows the associative law?
questions.hint: Work out both sides and see if the grouping changes the total.
questions.explanation: The associative law says that when three numbers are added (or multiplied), the way they are grouped does not change the answer: (3 + 4) + 5 = 7 + 5 = 12 and 3 + (4 + 5) = 3 + 9 = 12. It does not work for subtraction or division.

questions.question: Which expression is equal to 7 × 12 + 7 × 8 using the distributive law?
questions.hint: Look for the number that multiplies both terms and factor it out.
questions.explanation: The distributive law lets us factor out the shared number 7: 7 × 12 + 7 × 8 = 7 × (12 + 8) = 7 × 20 = 140.

questions.question: What is the smartest way to calculate 4 × 27 × 25 mentally?
questions.hint: Look for two numbers that combine to make a round number like 100.
questions.explanation: Using the commutative and associative laws, reorder to 4 × 25 × 27 = 100 × 27 = 2700. Multiplying 4 × 25 to make 100 first is far easier than multiplying in the original order.

questions.hint: Decide which operation happens first, then write brackets around it.
questions.explanation: 'Subtracts 5, then multiplies the result by 3' means the subtraction must happen first, so brackets are needed: (9 − 5) × 3 = 4 × 3 = 12.

questions.question: Work out 15 × 74.

questions.question: Evaluate 6 + 2 × (10 − 4) ÷ 3.

questions.explanation: Brackets first: 10 − 4 = 6, giving 6 + 2 × 6 ÷ 3. Multiplication and division next, left to right: 2 × 6 = 12, then 12 ÷ 3 = 4. Finally 6 + 4 = 10.

I can use brackets, including nested brackets, to control the order of a calculation.
I can apply the commutative law for addition and multiplication, and explain why subtraction and division are not commutative.
I can apply the associative law for addition and multiplication to group numbers efficiently.
I can apply the distributive law, a × (b + c) = (a × b) + (a × c), and use it in reverse to factor out a common number.
I can choose the smartest law to simplify a calculation and do more of it in my head.
I can translate word problems into expressions and check answers using a second method and estimation.
